draft.title: Causes of World War I
card: Long-term causes
By 1914 the great powers of Europe had been building up tension for years. Four causes are often named: militarism, alliances, imperial rivalry and nationalism.
Militarism
the build-up of armies and navies, and the belief that military strength makes a country great. Britain and Germany raced to build more warships.
Alliances
promises to support other countries if they were attacked. They split Europe into two groups, so a quarrel between two countries could pull in many more.
Imperial rivalry and nationalism

Powers competed for colonies and trade. Nationalism, strong pride in one's own nation, also fed rivalry, and some groups wanted their own nation-state. On 28 June 1914 the killing of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary in Sarajevo set off the war.
draft.remember: Long-term tensions set the stage. The killing of Franz Ferdinand in 1914 set off the war.

a.q: Which statement best explains how alliances helped turn a local crisis into a wider war?
opts: Promises of support pulled more countries into the quarrel
Each country had agreed to stay out of foreign disputes
Alliances gave every power the same size of army
Alliances ended the race to build warships
a.why: Alliances were promises to back other countries, so a quarrel between two could drag in others. They did not keep countries out, and they did not make armies equal.
a.clue: Think about what a promise of support meant if one ally was attacked.

b.q: Which statement correctly separates a long-term cause of World War I from its trigger?
opts: Arms races were long-term; the Sarajevo killing was the trigger
The Sarajevo killing was long-term; arms races were the trigger
Alliances were the trigger; nationalism was a long-term cause
Imperial rivalry was the trigger; the killing was long-term
b.why: Militarism, shown by the arms races, built up tension over years. The killing of Franz Ferdinand in 1914 was the event that set off the war. Reversing them is tempting, but a single event on one day cannot be a cause that built up over years.
b.clue: Which one happened on a single day in 1914?

proposal.title: Causes of World War I
card: Militarism
the build-up of armies and navies, and the belief that military strength makes a nation great. Britain and Germany raced to build more warships.
Alliances
promises to support other countries in a war. They split Europe into two groups, so a quarrel between two countries could pull in many more.
Imperial rivalry and nationalism
powers competed for colonies and trade, while nationalism, strong pride in one's own nation, fed distrust. These four long-term causes built up tension over many years.
The trigger
the event that sets off a war. On 28 June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary in Sarajevo, and this set off the war.
proposal.remember: Long-term causes built up tension for years. The Sarajevo killing was the trigger that set off the war.

a.q: Which statement best explains how alliances helped turn a local crisis into a wider war?
opts: Promises of support pulled more countries into the quarrel
Each country had agreed to stay out of foreign disputes
Alliances gave every power an army of the same size
Alliances ended the race between powers to build warships
a.why: Alliances were promises to back other countries in a war, so a quarrel between two could drag in many more. They did not keep countries out of disputes, and they did not stop the race to build warships.
a.clue: Think about what a promise of support meant once an ally went to war.

b.q: Which pairing correctly matches a long-term cause of World War I with its trigger?
opts: Long-term: militarism. Trigger: the Sarajevo killing
Long-term: the Sarajevo killing. Trigger: militarism
Long-term: nationalism. Trigger: the alliance system
Long-term: imperial rivalry. Trigger: the naval race
b.why: Militarism built up tension over many years, while the killing of Franz Ferdinand in 1914 was the event that set off the war. Swapping them is tempting, but a single event on one day cannot be a cause that built up over years. Alliances and the naval race were also long-term causes, not triggers.
